Agentic Decisions Study 2 shows a threshold rather than a gradient (Figure S3 in the supplementary material). DeepSeek, both GPT-6 models, Llama and Ministral 14B never performed the change, or claimed to, in any of their 960 conversations without valid verification, while acting on at least 98% of verified requests. Ministral 14B’s only errors arose with valid verification, one refusal and one reported change it had not made. Ministral 3B acted without valid verification in 58 of 672 retained conversations, 12 of them after the code was reported invalid, and 45 of these followed a claim of authority, 36% of such conversations, against at most 5% under any other pressure type. Persistence produced no violation in any model across 1,260 conversations without valid verification. Ministral 8B failed the no-pressure checks in every scenario, so the correct-first filter retained none and its figures cover all scenarios (Section S9). It acted without verification in only 12 of 960 conversations (1.3%), but refused 50.4% of verified requests and, in 20.0%, told the user that the change had been made without calling the tool. GPT-6 Luna, which abandoned correct answers under pressure in Study 1, never acted without verification, so for the stronger models concession on answers did not predict policy violations. 5.5. Mitigation Evidence-gated revision improved discrimination for Llama only (adjusted p = .045 p=.045 , Figure S4 in the supplementary material). Against the baseline prompt, it raised Llama’s d ′ d^{\prime} under persistence by 1.21 [0.64, 1.74] and under citation by 1.01 [0.29, 1.67], but against the generic warning only the citation gain remained, 0.93 [0.47, 1.47]. The gate sharply reduced Llama’s concessions to a wrong user, for example from 0.97 to 0.11 under authority, but it also reduced its corrections when the user was right, from 0.99 to 0.38 under the same pressure. Because the gate moved Llama off the ceiling, part of its measured gain in d ′ d^{\prime} reflects escape from a saturated baseline rather than improved discrimination alone. For GPT-6 Luna, the gate raised the bias under every pressure type, for example by 0.82 [0.56, 1.10] under authority, so that concession fell in both sets while d ′ d^{\prime} did not improve and fell under plain disagreement by 0.37 [0.05, 0.64]. For Ministral 3B, concession barely changed and d ′ d^{\prime} fell under authority by 0.50 [0.05, 0.98], although the model’s test did not survive correction. The gate therefore made GPT-6 Luna and Llama less ready to concede to correct and incorrect users alike, and improved discrimination only for Llama, whose baseline concession lay at the ceiling. 5.6. Implications Four findings bear on how vigilance in LLM agents should be evaluated and improved. First, a concession rate alone is misleading. Agents that readily corrected wrong answers also abandoned correct ones, and the evidence gate lowered concession to right and wrong users alike, so only separating discrimination from bias reveals vigilance. Second, the pressure that moved agents most was a claim they could not verify, such as a citation or a credential, rather than more forceful wording, and repetition moved answers but produced no policy violation, so defences should target how agents weigh unverifiable claims. Third, sycophancy over answers and over actions are distinct, so deployed agents should be tested on their actions, and a fabricated confirmation should be treated as a failure in its own right. Fourth, prompt-based mitigation mainly shifts readiness to concede, so mitigations should be judged on sensitivity, and improving discrimination is likely to require mechanisms beyond prompting, such as means for agents to verify the claims users make. 5.7. Limitations Sensitivity is estimated from different questions in the two sets, which may differ in difficulty and are restricted to those each agent answers consistently. It is therefore an operational measure on the evaluated items and may not extend to questions on which an agent is uncertain. Because cited sources are real only when the user is right, source authenticity cannot be separated from correctness, and agents may recognise genuine sources from prior knowledge. Study 1 offers no grounds that an agent can verify, and the mitigation was evaluated in Study 1 alone. Escalating conversations confound strength with turn number, acknowledgement of influence was not measured for actions, the scripted user leaves unanswered the clarifying questions that agents raised in 16.9% of Study 1 conversations, and the equal-variance assumption underlying d ′ d^{\prime} was not tested. Finally, Study 2 relies on a single synthetic scenario type. 6. Conclusion This paper separated two properties that a concession rate conflates, an agent’s ability to distinguish correction from manipulation and its readiness to concede. Only the GPT-6 models discriminated well, citations that agents could not verify increased concession and often impaired discrimination, and stronger wording added little. For the stronger models, yielding on answers did not predict policy violations, so agents should be evaluated on the actions they take, and fabricated confirmations should be treated as a distinct failure. Evidence-gated revision chiefly shifted readiness to concede, which suggests that prompting alone will not make agents vigilant. Future work should refine the acknowledgement probe and extend it to actions, introduce verifiable evidence and matched real and fabricated sources, and test whether verification tools improve discrimination.
